answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Alexander Hamilton wrote this to Robert Morris on April 30, 1781. His next sentence argues that debt could bind the Union together; the qualification “if it is not excessive” is part of the original.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: A national debt, if it is not excessive, will be to us a national blessing. It will be a powerful cement of our Union.
trail: The collected letter ↗ preserves both the qualification and Hamilton's following union argument.
Wikiquote ↗ identifies the same dated letter.
Sylla's historical discussion ↗ explains the wartime financial setting.
source.rightsNote: The eighteenth-century English letter is reproduced from an old collected edition and is public domain.

author.name: Alexander Hamilton
author.heading: About Alexander Hamilton
author.bio: Alexander Hamilton helped argue for the United States Constitution and became the first secretary of the Treasury. His earlier wartime correspondence already developed ideas about public credit and national finance.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Hamilton was considering a wartime financial system, not offering an unlimited endorsement of borrowing. The letter ↗ immediately links manageable debt with union and taxation; removing his condition about excess would change the argument.
